result.summary: Venus, seeing a plot against Julius Caesar, pleads with the gods, but Jove tells her Fate cannot be changed and foretells the rise of Augustus. Caesar is murdered in the Senate-house and Venus turns his soul into a star. Ovid praises Augustus, prays for his long life, and closes the poem by declaring his own work and name immortal.

scenes.title: Praise of Caesar and Augustus
scenes.summary: Ovid says Caesar's greatest deed was fathering Augustus, and that Caesar had to become a god so that Augustus would not be of mortal seed.

scenes.title: Venus pleads and omens appear
scenes.summary: Venus, alarmed at the plot, begs the gods for help. Portents warn of the crime, yet the conspirators strike in the Senate-house, and Venus tries to hide Caesar in a cloud.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears for Caesar's life and for her line descended from Iülus.

scenes.title: Jove reveals the Fates
scenes.summary: Jove tells Venus she cannot alter Fate. He foretells Augustus's victories, laws and eventual deification, and asks her to make Caesar's soul a star.
scenes.stakes: Venus must accept that Caesar's death is fated.

scenes.title: Caesar becomes a star
scenes.summary: Venus snatches Caesar's soul from his body and it becomes a comet. Ovid compares Augustus surpassing Caesar to other sons surpassing fathers.

scenes.title: Prayer and Ovid's epilogue
scenes.summary: Ovid prays the gods to keep Augustus long on earth, then claims his poem will outlast everything and make him immortal.
scenes.stakes: Ovid's own fame and survival after death.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Venus, from the island of Cythera.
Two forms of the Roman king of the gods' name.

notable_quotes.reason: Ovid's famous boast that his work will outlast Jove's anger, fire, steel and time.
Ovid claims his better part will rise immortal and his name be indelible.

analysis.text: The poem ends by linking mutability to permanence: Caesar's transformation into a star mirrors Ovid's claim that his verse transcends change.
The passage flatters Augustus and supports the cult of the deified Julius, whose comet appeared in 44 BC.

legacy.text: Ovid's closing boast of immortality echoes Horace's Odes and was imitated by later poets, such as Shakespeare in his sonnets.

fun_facts.text: Ovid was exiled by Augustus in AD 8, so this flattering ending was written shortly before his banishment.

language_notes.text: "He came a stranger to our temples" means Caesar was a newly admitted god, not an ancient native deity; "progeny" is Augustus, his adopted son.
People of Quirinus means the Romans; Quirinus is the deified Romulus. Juba and Mithridates were enemy kings defeated by Rome, Juba in Africa and Mithridates in Pontus.
Pontiff: Caesar was Pontifex Maximus, Rome's chief priest. Venus is called mother of Æneas, from whom the Julian family claimed descent.
At Troy Diomedes, son of Tydeus, wounded Venus with his spear while she was rescuing Æneas, as told in the Iliad.
The flames of Vesta were the sacred fire tended in Rome; Caesar's priesthood is linked to it, so his murder would put it out symbolically.
The aged sisters are the Fates, who spin and cut the thread of life; their decrees bind even the gods.
Lucifer is the morning star, Venus as seen before dawn, here dimmed by omen.
A liver lacking its head or extremity was a notorious bad sign in Roman divination by entrails.
Cytherea is a name for Venus, from the island of Cythera, linked to her cult.
The "three sisters" are the Fates, who spin, measure and cut the thread of life. Their archive of brass and iron symbolizes unchangeable destiny.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable substance, here used for the hardest, most enduring material.
"He" is Julius Caesar, assassinated in 44 BC. Cytherea is Venus, named for the island Cythera near where she was worshipped.
Mutina, Pharsalia, Philippi and the Sicilian waves refer to Roman civil-war battles. "One renowned as Great" is Sextus Pompey, son of Pompey the Great, defeated off Sicily.
The Egyptian dame is Cleopatra, wife of Antony in the translator's phrasing. Canopus is an Egyptian city, standing for Egypt; she is said to have threatened Rome's Capitol.
The "hallowed wife" is Livia; her son Tiberius was adopted by Augustus and took his name, securing the succession.
Augustus will reach old age, matching Caesar's years of glory, before joining the gods. The wording is compressed and ambiguous.
"These words" are Jupiter's speech just before, promising that Caesar will be deified. "Genial" here means kindly or life-giving, an epithet of Venus.
The star is the comet that appeared after Caesar's death in 44 BC, which Romans took as his soul ascending. Augustus (Caesar's adopted son) displayed it at games.
Atreus, Ægeus and Peleus are fathers outshone by their sons Agamemnon, Theseus and Achilles. Ovid uses these Greek examples to flatter Augustus.
Quirinus is the deified Romulus, founder of Rome; Gradivus is Mars, Romulus' father. Ovid calls Mars his son, following the Roman tradition.
"Tarpeian heights" means the Capitoline Hill in Rome, site of Jupiter's chief temple.
"Read by the lips of nations" refers to being read aloud, which was the usual way Romans experienced poetry.

context_notes.text: Julius Caesar was murdered in 44 BC in the Senate meeting place. A comet appeared soon after, and Romans took it as his soul ascending.
Caesar was stabbed in the Curia of Pompey, where the Senate was then meeting, on the Ides of March.
Jove is comforting Venus, whose descendant Julius Caesar has just been killed. She had tried to prevent the murder.
The son is Octavian, later Augustus, Caesar's adopted heir, who avenged his murder and was later honored as divine.
Caesar was deified after death; a comet appeared at his funeral games and was taken as his soul rising to heaven.
Caesar was assassinated in the Senate-house in 44 BC. Venus was regarded as ancestress of his family, the Julians, through her son Æneas.
Vesta, goddess of the hearth, had her sacred fire at Rome. Augustus, as pontifex maximus, placed a shrine to her in his house.
Ovid ends the Metamorphoses with this epilogue, claiming his poem as a monument. The closing echoes Horace's similar boast about his Odes.

literary_notes.text: The editorial summary anticipates the poet's closing boast of immortality, which Ovid makes in his own voice at the end of the poem.
A long catalogue of conquests is set against Augustus's parentage, so the question makes the answer, that fatherhood matters most, seem obvious, a flattering way to praise the emperor.
Venus's speech, addressed to the assembled gods, lets Ovid present Caesar's murder as a divine family crisis, heightening the pathos.
Repeated "often" piles up the omens, building a mood of dread around the coming murder.
"In a thousand places" is repeated and exaggerated, extending the catalogue of portents with hyperbolic force.
Echoing earlier rescues of Paris and Æneas in the cloud links Caesar's fate to Homeric epic, giving the event heroic weight.
Brass and iron tablets stand for the permanence and irreversibility of Fate, beyond even storms and lightning.
Jove prophesies in future tense events already past for Ovid's readers, flattering Augustus by making his victories seem fated.
Jove skips over the list of conquests, suggesting they are too numerous to tell and magnifying Augustus's reach.
Jove ends with a direct command to Venus, turning the prophecy into the action of Caesar's catasterism.
The comet's "flaming train" is presented as Caesar's soul, giving the heavenly body a human identity and fate.
Fame is a free, willful figure who ignores Augustus' commands, which also flatters him by showing his modesty.
The chain of father-and-son pairs climaxes with Saturn and Jove, raising Augustus' comparison to the level of the gods.
Ovid turns from narrative to address the gods directly in a long invocation, shifting the poem into formal prayer.
Ovid claims his poem is indestructible, listing forces of destruction in a sequence like a boast of monumental permanence.
The "better part" (his poetry and fame) is set against the perishable body, giving the epilogue its confident tone of immortality.
